title: Home to a hypergiant
caption: The super star cluster Westerlund 1, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Westerlund 1 · constellation Ara · about 15000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble looks at Westerlund 1, a young super star cluster about 15,000 light-years away. That may sound enormous, but on an astronomical scale it is close, since an object at that distance still lies within our own galaxy, the Milky Way.

Among its members is one of the largest stars ever found, first named Westerlund 1-26. Astronomers identified it while classifying the cluster's stars by spectral type, temperature and brightness. It is a red supergiant, sometimes classed as a hypergiant, with a radius more than 1500 times the Sun's. Placed where the Sun is, it would reach beyond the orbit of Jupiter.

Most of the cluster's stars are thought to have formed in a single burst, so they share similar ages and compositions. At around three million years old, the cluster is a baby next to the Sun, whose age is some 4.6 billion years.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (4.13 x 3.93 arcminutes) and distance (15000 light years), the frame spans roughly 18 × 17 light-years. Its light set out about 15,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed the cluster in near-infrared light through three filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: All three filters record near-infrared light, which is invisible to the human eye.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.

explore: Light moves at just under 300 000 kilometres per second. A light-year, despite the name, is a distance, the length light travels in a year, around nine trillion kilometres.
alt: A young super star cluster seen in near-infrared light.
